articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.summary: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype.
body: The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.

For many players, meanwhile, the 13-year wait for a new Grand Theft Auto has become unbearable. When footage of GTA VI made its glitzy premiere on Netflix, it almost took the streaming giant’s servers down. Its first trailer has been viewed 300m times on YouTube alone. Across the world, people have booked days off work on 19 November to experience this event together – one of those increasingly rare shared global cultural moments in an age when we all live in our own algorithmic content bubbles.

articles.title: 160 questions, only one wrong: top scorer in South Korea tax exam admits AI cheating
articles.summary: Fears for national college entrance exam next week as test taker admits sending photos of questions to AI tool. The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true.
body: The scandal follows months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July. It has also raised the stakes for organisers of South Korea’s annual college entrance exam this Thursday.

“I cheated using ⁠electronic devices and generative AI. My passing the exam with the top score was not ​the result of fair effort,” the candidate said, ‌identifying himself by the ‌surname Han, as he apologised on the YouTube channel Attorney Lee Don-ho.

Han, who ranked first in both rounds of the qualification exam held in April and July, confessed through his lawyer that he used AI to obtain answers during the tests. He said he had cheated by ‌taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an AI tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.
His score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, with only one wrong answer out of 160 questions, had sparked accusations that he cheated using smart glasses, which he initially denied.

articles.title: This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets
articles.summary: A Carnegie Mellon student’s tiny E Ink gadgets, called OATs, give houseplants, skateboards, and dumbbells expressive personalities to nudge you toward better habits.
body: You forgot to water the plant. Instead of seeing yellowing leaves, you see a cute plant-shaped pet on a tiny screen, looking sad and dejected. Maybe that'll give you the push you needed to grab the watering can. As you pour water into the soil, the plant pet on the screen gets excited and happy.

That's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects. The tech was created by Daehwa Kim, a fifth-year PhD student in Carnegie Mellon's Future Interfaces Group. Kim presented the project at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in Detroit in early November, a forum where academics and industry experts explore human-computer interfaces, and she earned two Honorable Mention awards.

articles.title: ‘Prove you are not a robot’: how the Captcha scam captures your computer
articles.summary: Unlike familiar Captcha tests, this con asks you to press a series of keys. And that’s a way in for fraudsters to install malicious software. You are looking for some gifts for Christmas and want to support small businesses when you shop.
body: Instead of clicking on a series of images, or typing letters that appear, just as you have seen before, you are asked to press a series of keys and then press enter.

This is a tactic known as the “ClickFix” scam one of the most popular used by criminals to trick people into infecting their own computer with malicious software, according to Chris Fistonich, a researcher with cybersecurity company Malwarebytes.

“ClickFix is really one of the most sophisticated malware campaigns there is,” he says. “People are not prepared for this. They are used to solving Captchas every day. They’re used to being able to trust their security software. So it really has opened a new security loophole that’s being exploited extensively.”
He adds: “This is the most popular way to get malware on to your computer. Certainly not the only way, but today it is definitely the most popular.”

And that’s a way in for fraudsters to install malicious software.

articles.title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
articles.summary: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true. The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs…
body: Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet.

The scandal has thrown Nvidia into crisis, cast a pall over the AI boom and even threatened the stability of the US economy. Huang’s downfall is a nightmare scenario for a tech industry that has become increasingly fearful of security threats, and a glimpse into what intelligence experts say is a constant theater of corporate espionage secretly playing out every day throughout the US.

“The reason that this is making the news is because obviously you have one of the wealthiest men in the world and one of the highest-profile CEOs in the world,” said Don Aviv, the CEO of corporate intelligence firm Interfor International. “But this happens all the time, across industries.”
points: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true.

articles.title: It’s Getting Too Dry for Even Cactuses to Survive
articles.summary: As droughts worsen due to climate change, new research shows that hundreds of cactus species could lose the majority of their habitats by 2100.
body: The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.

Yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled a future of not just relentlessly rising temperatures but also the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.

“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing—and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly—but they’re not that different from other plants.”
points: As droughts worsen due to climate change, new research shows that hundreds of cactus species could lose the majority of their habitats by 2100.

articles.title: Evercade Nexus Review: The Best Retro Handheld Yet
articles.summary: Evercade’s best handheld yet is a major level-up for the retro specialist.
body: Specialist hardware manufacturer Blaze Entertainment has spent the 2020s quietly carving out a niche for itself as the go-to option for retro gaming. With a stable of reliable hardware, from the original Evercade handheld to the Evercade Alpha bartop arcade cabinet, it offers numerous ways to play, all built around an ever-expanding library of physical cartridges. Each brings a curated selection of classic titles and lost curiosities to modern players.

The Evercade Nexus is more than just the latest addition to its console lineup. While it retains compatibility with every previously released Evercade cartridge, it’s also the biggest leap forward the line has taken so far, both in hardware and in what it might offer with games going forward. It’s a real level up—and it’s rather brilliant.

The most obvious change is the sheer size. Where Blaze’s previous handhelds were about on par with the original Game Boy Advance, aimed at pocketable play, the Evercade Nexus is closer in scale to a Nintendo Switch Lite. It measures 215 x 111 x 34 millimeters and weighs 410 grams—still easily portable, but more in the “buy a protective hard case and throw it in your bag” kind of way.
points: Evercade’s best handheld yet is a major level-up for the retro specialist.

articles.title: SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch
articles.summary: STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position.
body: Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms.

Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket.

This was a breathtaking feat; a brilliant technical achievement that required the best engineering minds to think through a million different, difficult problems. And on Saturday evening, following a handful of practice runs into the Indian Ocean, they did it before the entire world.

Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power, and be captured by the tower.

articles.title: Logitech Yeti 2 Review: An All-In-One Studio Setup
articles.summary: The follow-up to the iconic Yeti microphone is here, and its upgrades make it worthy of the legacy.
body: The original Blue Yeti microphone was first released in 2009, and it remains the most ubiquitous microphone for home recording 17 years later. Chances are, if you’ve watched a YouTube video, Twitch stream, or listened to a podcast, you’ve heard (and probably seen) this microphone at least once.

Long after absorbing Blue and phasing out the brand name, Logitech has finally released its highly anticipated successor: the Yeti 2. The follow-up maintains the same general shape and look but drastically changes the microphone’s functionality. Instead of simply recording audio, the Yeti 2 has a handful of features to monitor and manipulate the audio passing through it, seamlessly recording production-quality audio with zero delay. While some of the design feels a bit underdeveloped, the Yeti 2 is a deserving sequel to the iconic original model and an easy shoe-in as the best USB microphone you can buy.

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering is getting a Netflix animated series. For real this time.
articles.summary: "It's really happening. I promise. For real." Those are the first words from Roy Graham, Head of Story at Magic: The Gathering, in a video posted yesterday announcing Planeswalker, the animated series heading to Netflix in 2027.
body: Magic The Gathering: Planeswalker is set to debut on Netflix in 2027.

An animated Magic: The Gathering series was first teased back in 2019 with Joe and Anthony Russo at the helm. But that fell apart. In 2024, Netflix announced it still planned to make a series based on the game, but it decided to rework it from the ground up.

Now fans are finally getting their first glimpse of the show, which will be called Planeswalker. According to the sneak peek, because each plane exists in its own pocket universe, it will have a unique design, animation, and filmmaking style.

According to a synopsis of the show shared with IGN, Planeswalker will focus on Chandra Nalaar, a “volatile pyromancer hunted for her gifts, and haunted by her past.” Storyline details beyond that are vague, other than mentioning an “insidious force” that Chandra and other Planeswalkers will team up to confront “to prevent a cataclysmic war that threatens to consume their very existence.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang Carried a Secret for More Than a Year. It Led to His Downfall.
articles.summary: Nvidia’s leader said his relationship with a female customer was just about business. But what he was concealing eventually led to his resignation from the company he created.
body: It was September 2025, and The New York Times had just called his company about a Singaporean data center firm called Megaspeed that had been led by a Chinese woman named Alice Huang, or Huang Le. The Times was reporting that Mr. Huang, the chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, had a close relationship with her.

Mr. Huang, who Nvidia employees say could have a volcanic temper, wanted to know what The Times was insinuating. Though he didn’t deny that he knew the woman, he was bothered by the suggestion that they might be close, people familiar with the discussion said.

Nvidia mounted an aggressive defense. Madison Huang, Mr. Huang’s daughter who acted as her father’s chief of staff, pressed the company’s communications team to push back forcefully. They also had reinforcements, a crisis communications firm called Heller.
They insisted that Mr. Huang and the woman from Megaspeed just had a business relationship.
points: Nvidia’s leader said his relationship with a female customer was just about business.
But what he was concealing eventually led to his resignation from the company he created.
